0.title: Knowing the God Who Is
0.overview:
Every person has a picture of God. Some picture a stern judge, some a distant force, some an indulgent friend who never minds what we do. Most of us carry a mixture of all three, shaped more by our upbringing and our moods than by the Bible. And the picture matters, because we become like what we worship, and we trust only as far as we know.

The attributes of God are the truths Scripture tells us about what God is like: that he is eternal, unchanging, everywhere present, all-knowing, all-powerful, wise, just, good, loving, merciful, patient and faithful. They are not a list of abstract properties for theologians. They are God's own self-introduction. When Moses asked to see God's glory, God answered by proclaiming his name and his character (Exod 34:6-7). To know the attributes of God is to know God as he has chosen to be known.

This matters for the most practical reasons. A Christian facing a frightening diagnosis needs to know that God is all-powerful and all-wise. A believer who has failed badly needs to know that God is merciful and patient. A Christian who has been wronged needs to know that God is just. A grieving widow needs to know that God is faithful and does not change. Almost every struggle of the Christian life is, at bottom, a question about what God is like.

Six units: (1) How God Makes Himself Known; (2) God in himself: Eternal, Independent, Unchanging; (3) Everywhere, All-Knowing, All-Powerful; (4) Righteous and Wrathful; (5) Love, Goodness, Mercy and Patience; (6) Faithful and True. Three of God's attributes have studies of their own: the Holiness of God, the Grace of God and the Sovereignty of God. This study gathers the rest and shows how they all belong together in the one living God.

1.title: How God Makes Himself Known
1.overview:
We cannot discover God by our own cleverness. He is infinite and we are finite; he is the Creator and we are creatures. If we are to know him at all, he must make himself known. And he has. The heavens declare his glory (Ps 19:1), and his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived in the things he has made (Rom 1:20). But creation tells us only so much. In Scripture God speaks, and in Jesus Christ he comes in person: Whoever has seen me has seen the Father (John 14:9).

The richest Old Testament description of God comes at a dark moment. Israel had just worshipped the golden calf. Moses pleaded with God not to abandon his people and asked, Please show me your glory (Exod 33:18). God hid him in a cleft of the rock and passed by, proclaiming his name: The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod 34:6). This self-description echoes through the rest of the Bible, in the Psalms, in the prophets and in Jonah's complaint. God's glory, it turns out, is above all his character.

Notice what God emphasises. Mercy, grace, patience, steadfast love and faithfulness come first and are described at length. Justice is there too: he will by no means clear the guilty (Exod 34:7). Both are real. Neither cancels the other. But God wants to be known first as the God who abounds in steadfast love.

Scripture also tells us that knowing God is the purpose of our lives. Let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me (Jer 9:24). Jesus defines eternal life itself in these terms: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). To study the attributes of God is not a detour from the Christian life. It is the heart of it.
1.theology:
Attributes only God has, and attributes he shares: Christians have long distinguished two kinds of attribute. Some belong to God alone: that he depends on nothing, never changes, is eternal and is present everywhere. We will never share these. Others God shares, in a creaturely measure, with those made in his image: wisdom, goodness, love, mercy, justice, holiness and faithfulness. The first kind teaches us humility and worship. The second teaches us what God is making us into (Eph 5:1).

God is not made of parts: God's attributes are not pieces that add up to God, as if he were partly loving and partly just. Every attribute is a description of the whole God. His love is a just love, and his justice is a loving justice. His power is always wise, and his wisdom is always powerful. This is why we must never set one attribute against another, as though God's love had to overcome his holiness.

Known truly, never fully: We can know God truly because he has spoken truly. But we will never know him exhaustively, even in eternity. How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! (Rom 11:33). Mystery is not a failure of our theology. It is what we should expect when creatures speak of their Creator.
1.examples:
Then: Jonah knew the attributes of God well, and they made him angry. When God spared Nineveh, Jonah prayed, I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love (Jonah 4:2). He was quoting Exodus 34. Jonah had the right doctrine and the wrong heart. Knowing God's attributes is meant to make us love what God loves, even his mercy to our enemies.

Now: A young Christian realises that her picture of God came mostly from her father, who was hard to please and quick to criticise. She has always assumed that God is disappointed in her. As she reads Exodus 34 and Psalm 103 slowly, she begins to see that she has been worshipping a God who does not exist. The real God is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love. Her obedience does not stop. But it begins to come from gratitude rather than fear.

A simple test: Finish the sentence, "God is the kind of God who..." Then ask whether your answer comes from Scripture or from your experience.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD passed before him and proclaimed, "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children and the children's children, to the third and the fourth generation." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is God's own definition of himself, given to Moses after Israel's greatest betrayal. Almost all of it speaks of mercy. Yet the last lines are sobering: God will by no means clear the guilty. How can a God who forgives iniquity also refuse to clear the guilty? The Old Testament leaves the tension standing. The cross resolves it: there God forgave sinners because he punished their sin in his Son (Rom 3:26).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the LORD who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight, declares the LORD." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Wisdom, strength and wealth are the three great boasts of the world. God sets them all aside. The one thing worth boasting in is knowing him. And notice what he wants to be known for: steadfast love, justice, and righteousness. And notice too that he delights in these. God's attributes are not grudging duties. They are what he loves to do.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus does not say eternal life is the reward for knowing God. He says it is knowing God. Eternal life is a relationship before it is a length of time. And this knowledge comes only through the Son: the true God is known as we know Jesus Christ whom you have sent. Every attribute of God is seen most clearly in the face of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! "For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?" "Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?" For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul has just spent eleven chapters explaining God's plan of salvation. His response is not a summary but a song. The more he understands, the more he realises how much is beyond him. God has no counsellor and owes no one anything; everything is from him and through him and to him. Good theology always ends here, in doxology.

1.reflection:
Where did your first picture of God come from? Which parts of it are biblical, and which are not?

Read Exodus 34:6-7 aloud. Which phrase do you most need to believe this week?

Why is it dangerous to set one of God's attributes against another?

How does Jesus show you what God is like? Choose one scene from the Gospels.

2.title: God in Himself: Eternal, Independent, Unchanging
2.overview:
When Moses asked for God's name at the burning bush, God answered, I AM WHO I AM (Exod 3:14). Everything else in the universe is what it is because something else made it so. God simply is. He is not becoming, not growing, not depending on anything outside himself. He is the one fixed point of reality.

God is independent. He needs nothing. Paul told the philosophers of Athens that God is not served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything (Acts 17:25). God did not create the world because he was lonely or incomplete. The Father, the Son and the Spirit lived in perfect love before anything was made (John 17:24). He created out of overflowing goodness, not need. This is deeply freeing. We cannot add to God, and we cannot diminish him. Our worship does not supply something he lacks; it brings us into the joy he already has.

God is eternal. From everlasting to everlasting you are God (Ps 90:2). He had no beginning and will have no end. He is not trapped in time as we are, waiting for the future to arrive. He made time and rules over it. With the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day (2 Pet 3:8). For mortals whose lives are like grass, this is the only safe place to stand: Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations (Ps 90:1).

God is unchanging. For I the LORD do not change; therefore you, O children of Jacob, are not consumed (Mal 3:6). God does not grow wiser, kinder or stronger, because he is already infinitely all three. He does not grow weaker, more forgetful or less patient. His character, his purposes and his promises stand. James calls him the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change (Jas 1:17). The sun moves and shadows shift. God does not.

This does not mean God is cold or static. He acts, speaks, rescues and judges. He responds to prayer. But he always acts as the same God, according to the same character and the same eternal plan.
2.theology:
"God relented": the views. Several passages say that God relented or regretted (Gen 6:6; Exod 32:14; Jonah 3:10). Yet Samuel says God is not a man, that he should have regret (1 Sam 15:29), in the very chapter where God says he regrets making Saul king (1 Sam 15:11). Some conclude that God genuinely changes his mind as events unfold, because he does not know or has not settled the future. Others hold that God never changes in his character or his eternal purpose, and that "relenting" describes a real change in how he deals with people when they change, a change he himself planned and announced.

The verdict: The second view fits all the texts. God himself explains the pattern: if a nation he has threatened turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it (Jer 18:8). His warnings carry a condition, stated or unstated. When Nineveh repented, God did exactly what his unchanging character had always promised to do. The language of relenting is real language about real events, but it is spoken from our side of the story. It never means God was surprised, mistaken or fickle.

Does God feel? The historic confessions describe God as "without body, parts, or passions." Some take this to mean God is unmoved and unfeeling. Others, reacting, say God suffers and changes emotionally as we do. The better view stands between them: God does not undergo moods forced on him from outside, but his love, joy, compassion and anger are real and perfect, the settled responses of his unchanging character. The Son, having taken human nature, truly wept and suffered.
2.examples:
Then: Psalm 90 is called A Prayer of Moses, the man of God. Moses had buried a whole generation in the wilderness. He knew how short life is: The years of our life are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty (Ps 90:10). His comfort was not that life would last longer, but that God lasts forever. He asks the eternal God to establish the work of our hands (Ps 90:17), so that brief lives would have lasting meaning.

Now: A man in his seventies has seen almost everything change: his body, his career, his church, his country, his friendships. Many of those he loved are gone. One evening he reads Malachi 3:6 and Hebrews 13:8, Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. For the first time in years he feels steady ground under his feet. Everything else has moved. God has not.

A simple test: When your circumstances change suddenly, what do you instinctively assume about God? That he has changed toward you, or that he is the same?

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses said to God, "If I come to the people of Israel and say to them, 'The God of your fathers has sent me to you,' and they ask me, 'What is his name?' what shall I say to them?" God said to Moses, "I AM WHO I AM." And he said, "Say this to the people of Israel: 'I AM has sent me to you.'" God also said to Moses, "Say this to the people of Israel: 'The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.' This is my name forever, and thus I am to be remembered throughout all generations. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses wanted a name to give the enslaved Israelites. God gave him a name that is also a statement: I AM WHO I AM. The God who sends Moses depends on no one and answers to no one. And yet this same God immediately ties himself to people: the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. The self-existent God is the covenant God. Jesus took this name on his own lips: before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58).

verseByVerse.quote: The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man, nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Athens was full of temples, statues and offerings, all built on the assumption that the gods needed looking after. Paul turns the idea upside down. God does not need us; we need him for every breath. This is humbling, but it is also good news. A God who needs nothing can never be manipulated, bribed or exhausted. He gives because he is generous, not because he is in our debt.

verseByVerse.quote: "For I the LORD do not change; therefore you, O children of Jacob, are not consumed. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Malachi's hearers had grown careless and cynical. They deserved to be consumed. The only reason they had not been is that God does not change. He had made promises to Jacob, and he would keep them. God's unchangeableness is not a cold fact; it is the reason sinners survive. If God's love depended on our steadiness, we would be lost. It depends on his.

verseByVerse.quote: God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not fulfill it? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Balaam was hired to curse Israel. Each time he tried, God made him bless them instead. Here he explains why the king who hired him cannot get what he wants: God does not lie or change his mind the way people do. Has he said, and will he not do it? Every promise God makes rests on this verse. What he has said, he will do.

2.reflection:
How does it change your prayers to know that God needs nothing from you?

Read Psalm 90. What does Moses ask for in light of God's eternity and our shortness of life?

How would you explain Jonah 3:10 to someone who thinks it proves God changes his mind?

What changes in your life are unsettling you? Which unchanging truth about God speaks to them?

3.title: Everywhere, All-Knowing, All-Powerful
3.overview:
Psalm 139 is the Bible's great meditation on three attributes that belong to God alone. And remarkably, David does not treat them as abstract ideas. He prays them.

God knows everything. O LORD, you have searched me and known me! You know when I sit down and when I rise up; you discern my thoughts from afar (Ps 139:1-2). God knows our actions, our words before we speak them and our thoughts before we think them. He knows the number of the stars (Ps 147:4) and the hairs on our heads (Matt 10:30). He knows the future as surely as the past: declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done (Isa 46:10). Nothing has ever occurred to God. Nothing has ever surprised him.

God is everywhere. Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? (Ps 139:7). Heaven, the grave, the far side of the sea, the darkness: God is there. This does not mean God is spread thinly through the universe like a gas, or that everything is God. It means the whole God is present to every part of his creation. Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the LORD (Jer 23:24).

God can do all that he wills. Ah, Lord GOD! It is you who have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm! Nothing is too hard for you (Jer 32:17). God's power is not force without direction. It is always the power of his wisdom and goodness. There are things God cannot do: he cannot lie (Heb 6:18), cannot deny himself (2 Tim 2:13) and cannot be tempted with evil (Jas 1:13). These are not limits on his power. They are the perfections of his character.

For the unrepentant, these truths are terrifying. No creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account (Heb 4:13). For believers, they are the deepest comfort. The God who knows everything about us has loved us anyway. The God who is everywhere is with us in the hospital room and the lonely flat. The God who can do anything is on our side.
3.theology:
Does God know the future? The views. Some modern teachers, called open theists, argue that God cannot know the free choices people have not yet made, because those choices do not yet exist to be known. On this view God takes risks, learns as history unfolds and sometimes is disappointed. Historic Christianity holds that God knows all things, past, present and future, including every free choice, because he is the eternal Creator and Lord of history.

The verdict: Scripture is clear and repeated. God predicts free human actions centuries in advance, from Cyrus by name (Isa 45:1) to Peter's denial that very night (Matt 26:34). He knew every one of our days when as yet there was none of them (Ps 139:16). In Isaiah, the ability to declare the future is the very thing that proves the LORD is God and the idols are not (Isa 41:22-23). A God who did not know the future could not promise anything with certainty. Open theism removes the ground of every promise.

Wisdom: Knowing everything is not the same as being wise. Wisdom is choosing the best ends and the best means. God is the only wise God (Rom 16:27), and his wisdom is seen above all in the cross, which looks like foolishness to the world (1 Cor 1:24-25).
3.examples:
Then: Hagar ran away from Sarai's harsh treatment into the desert, alone and pregnant. There the angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water. She gave God a name: You are a God of seeing (Gen 16:13). A runaway slave woman in the wilderness discovered that she was not invisible. God saw her.

Now: A teenager struggling with a secret sin reads Psalm 139 and feels exposed. God knows all of it. A wise pastor helps him read on to the end of the psalm, where David asks God to search him and lead me in the way everlasting (Ps 139:24). The God who sees everything is not waiting to shame him. He is ready to lead him out.

A simple test: Does the thought that God sees everything make you want to hide or to come near? The gospel is meant to turn the first into the second.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, you have searched me and known me! You know when I sit down and when I rise up; you discern my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down and are acquainted with all my ways. Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O LORD, you know it altogether. You hem me in, behind and before, and lay your hand upon me. Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high; I cannot attain it. Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there! If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me. If I say, "Surely the darkness shall cover me, and the light about me be night," even the darkness is not dark to you; the night is bright as the day, for darkness is as light with you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: David begins with God's knowledge (vv. 1-6) and moves to his presence (vv. 7-12). His first reaction is something like being overwhelmed: Such knowledge is too wonderful for me. He imagines fleeing to the heights, the depths and the farthest sea, and finds God already there. Even darkness does not hide him, for darkness is as light with you. There is no place where God is absent, and so no place where his people are alone.

verseByVerse.quote: "Am I a God at hand, declares the LORD, and not a God far away? Can a man hide himself in secret places so that I cannot see him? declares the LORD. Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: False prophets in Jeremiah's day spoke lies in God's name as if he could not hear them. God answers with three questions. He is not a local deity confined to one place; he is near and far at once. No one can hide in a secret place from him. He fills heaven and earth. Those who speak for God must remember that God is listening.

verseByVerse.quote: remember the former things of old; for I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like me, declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, 'My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose,' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Babylon's idols had to be carried on the backs of animals (Isa 46:1). The LORD is the opposite: he carries his people (Isa 46:4). Here he gives his credentials. He alone declares the end from the beginning, and his counsel stands. History is not a series of accidents God tries to manage. It is the unfolding of his purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Ah, Lord GOD! It is you who have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm! Nothing is too hard for you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jerusalem was under siege, and God told Jeremiah to buy a field, a land deal that seemed absurd with the Babylonians at the gates. Jeremiah obeyed, then prayed. He begins with creation: the God who made heaven and earth can certainly restore a ruined land. Nothing is too hard for you. God later echoes the words back to him (Jer 32:27). Faith often means acting on God's power before we can see how he will use it.

3.reflection:
Read Psalm 139:1-18. Which verse is most comforting to you, and which most unsettling?

How would you answer someone who says God cannot know our future choices?

Where do you need to remember this week that God is present with you?

Why are the things God cannot do signs of his perfection rather than his weakness?

4.title: Righteous and Wrathful
4.overview:
Many people today are happy to believe in a loving God but recoil from a God of justice and wrath. Yet the Bible's God is both, and if he were not just, he would not be good.

God is righteous. The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice. A God of faithfulness and without iniquity, just and upright is he (Deut 32:4). God always does what is right. He never takes bribes, never shows favouritism and never punishes the innocent or acquits the guilty. When Abraham pleaded for Sodom, he appealed to this: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? (Gen 18:25).

God is wrathful. God's wrath is his settled, holy opposition to evil. It is not a temper tantrum or wounded pride. It is what love and justice look like when they meet cruelty, lies and rebellion. A God who looked at child abuse, genocide and human trafficking and felt nothing would not be loving. For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men (Rom 1:18). God's wrath is present now, as he hands people over to the sins they choose (Rom 1:24), and it will be revealed fully on the last day (Rom 2:5).

God is jealous. The LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God (Exod 34:14). Human jealousy is often petty, but there is a right jealousy, the jealousy of a husband for his wife's faithfulness. God will not share his people's love with idols, because idols destroy those who worship them.

The cross is where justice and mercy meet. If God simply overlooked sin, he would cease to be just. If he punished every sinner, no one would be saved. At the cross God did both. He put forward his Son as a propitiation by his blood, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Rom 3:25-26). Jesus drank the cup of wrath so that those who trust in him never will. Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God (Rom 5:9).
4.theology:
Wrath is not the opposite of love: The opposite of love is indifference. God's wrath and his love both flow from his holiness. He is angry at sin because he loves what sin destroys. And his wrath, unlike his love, is never described as his delight. He is slow to anger but abounding in steadfast love (Exod 34:6).

Hell: the views. Some evangelicals hold that the unrepentant will finally be destroyed and cease to exist. The historic view is that they will suffer conscious punishment forever. The verdict: Jesus sets the two destinies side by side with the same word: these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life (Matt 25:46). If the life is endless, so is the punishment. Jesus spoke of hell more than anyone in Scripture, and he did so with tears for those he warned (Luke 19:41).

Justice for the wronged: God's justice is good news for victims. Those who have suffered great wrongs need not take revenge, because God will repay (Rom 12:19). No crime is ever finally lost or forgotten. Every wrong will either be paid for at the cross or answered at the judgment.
4.examples:
Then: Nahum's prophecy is a sustained announcement of God's wrath on Nineveh, the capital of an empire that had terrorised the nations for generations. For the Assyrians it was terrible news. For the peoples they had crushed it was comfort: The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble (Nah 1:7). The same justice that terrifies the oppressor shelters the oppressed.

Now: A woman who was wronged years ago by a business partner who was never held to account has carried a quiet rage ever since. Learning that God is just does two things for her. It assures her that the wrong matters and will be answered. And it frees her from the job of making sure it is. She can leave it with the Judge of all the earth.

A simple test: Do you find it easier to believe in God's justice for others or in his mercy for yourself? The cross requires both.

verseByVerse.quote: Far be it from you to do such a thing, to put the righteous to death with the wicked, so that the righteous fare as the wicked! Far be that from you! Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Abraham bargains with God over Sodom, from fifty righteous people down to ten. His boldness rests on one conviction: God will not treat the righteous and the wicked alike. He is not trying to make God more just than he is. He is appealing to the justice God already has. Every prayer for justice in a broken world stands on this question.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is a jealous and avenging God; the LORD is avenging and wrathful; the LORD takes vengeance on his adversaries and keeps wrath for his enemies. The LORD is slow to anger and great in power, and the LORD will by no means clear the guilty. His way is in whirlwind and storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: These verses hold together what we tend to separate. God is jealous, avenging and wrathful. He is also slow to anger. Nineveh had received a reprieve in Jonah's day, a century and more before. God's patience is real, but it is not endless. Those who presume on it will find that he will by no means clear the guilty.

verseByVerse.quote: For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's great explanation of the gospel begins not with God's love but with his wrath. This is not because wrath is more important. It is because the good news makes no sense until we see the bad news. People suppress the truth about God that they know, and God's wrath is already revealed as he lets them go their own way.

verseByVerse.quote: whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith. This was to show God's righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins. It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is the answer to the riddle of Exodus 34:7. How can God forgive iniquity and yet not clear the guilty? By putting forward Christ as a propitiation, a sacrifice that turns away wrath by bearing it. God's past patience with sin was not injustice; it looked ahead to the cross. Now God is both just and the justifier. He did not lower his standard to save us. He met it himself.

4.reflection:
Why would a God without wrath against evil be less loving, not more?

How does Romans 3:25-26 answer the tension in Exodus 34:6-7?

Is there a wrong done to you that you need to leave with the Judge of all the earth?

How should the reality of hell shape the way you speak about Christ to others?

5.title: Love, Goodness, Mercy and Patience
5.overview:
God is love (1 John 4:8). This is one of the shortest and most profound sentences in the Bible. It does not mean that love is God, so that whatever we feel as love is divine. It means that love is not something God does occasionally, but something he is. Before creation, the Father loved the Son (John 17:24). Love is the life of the Trinity, and God's love for us overflows from it.

John tells us where to look to see this love: In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins (1 John 4:10). God's love is not a feeling we must detect in our hearts. It is a fact accomplished in history. When we doubt God's love, we do not look inward. We look at the cross.

God is good. The LORD is good to all, and his mercy is over all that he has made (Ps 145:9). Every meal, sunrise, friendship and breath is a gift of his goodness, given to believers and unbelievers alike (Matt 5:45).

God is merciful. Mercy is God's goodness toward those who are suffering or who deserve punishment. He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities (Ps 103:10). As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him (Ps 103:13).

God is patient. He is slow to anger. He bears with sinners for years, giving them time to repent. Peter explains the apparent delay of Christ's return in these terms: God is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Pet 3:9). Every day the world goes on is a day of God's patience.

These attributes are not soft spots in an otherwise stern God. They are what he chose to proclaim first when he revealed his glory (Exod 34:6). Grace, the free favour of God to the undeserving, belongs here too and has a study of its own.
5.theology:
Kinds of divine love: Scripture speaks of God's love in more than one way. He loves all that he has made and is good to all (Ps 145:9). He loves the world enough to send his Son and to call all people to repent (John 3:16; Acts 17:30). And he has a particular, saving love for his people, the love with which Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Eph 5:25). Confusing these leads to error. Denying the first makes God cold toward the lost; denying the last makes his love vague and powerless.

Love and wrath together: God's love does not cancel his wrath; it provides the answer to it. Love that never opposed evil would be indifference. Wrath without love would leave us without hope. At the cross, God's love bore God's wrath.

Patience has a purpose: God's patience is meant to lead us to repentance (Rom 2:4). To treat it as permission to keep sinning is to despise it. The day of patience will end.
5.examples:
Then: In Jesus' parable, the younger son wasted his inheritance and came home rehearsing a speech about being made a servant. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him (Luke 15:20). Jesus told the story to show what God is like toward repentant sinners.

Now: A Christian man has been praying for an unbelieving brother for thirty years. He is tempted to give up. Reading 2 Peter 3:9, he realises that God has been more patient with his brother than he has, and was patient with him too, through years of his own wandering. He keeps praying.

A simple test: When you sin, do you run from God or to him? Your answer shows what you really believe about his mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love. In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him. In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: John's logic is simple: if God is love, those who know him will love. But he anchors this in what God has done, not in what we feel. God's love is seen in sending his only Son, so that we might live. And it is love for the unloving: not that we have loved God but that he loved us. We do not earn God's love by loving him. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love. He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever. He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities. For as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is his steadfast love toward those who fear him; as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us. As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him. For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: David quotes Exodus 34 and then explains it with pictures. God's anger does not last forever. His steadfast love is as high as the heavens. He removes our transgressions as far as the east is from the west. He is compassionate like a father. And he remembers that we are dust. God is not surprised by our weakness. He made us, and he deals with us gently.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love. The LORD is good to all, and his mercy is over all that he has made. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Psalm 145 again echoes Exodus 34, and then widens the circle. God's mercy is over all that he has made. This is the goodness theologians call common grace: rain, harvest, health, beauty, family and the restraint of evil, given to the whole world. Every unbeliever lives every day on the kindness of the God he ignores.

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Scoffers asked why Christ had not returned. Peter's answer is that God's timing is not slowness but patience. Every year of delay is another year for people to repent. God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezek 33:11). The church's task in the meantime is to call people to Christ while the door is open.

5.reflection:
Where do you look when you doubt God's love? Where does 1 John 4:10 tell you to look?

Read Psalm 103 slowly. Which picture of God's mercy means most to you, and why?

Name three gifts of God's goodness you received today without thinking about it.

Who are you tempted to give up on? How does God's patience with you change that?

6.title: Faithful and True
6.overview:
Jerusalem had fallen. The temple was burned, the people were starving and the survivors were led away in chains. In the middle of the bleakest book in the Bible, the poet writes, The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness (Lam 3:22-23). He did not say this because things were going well. He said it because God is faithful even when everything else has collapsed.

God is true. He cannot lie (Titus 1:2; Heb 6:18). Everything he says is reliable. Jesus prayed, your word is truth (John 17:17). This is why Scripture can be trusted completely: it is the word of a God who does not deceive.

God is faithful. He keeps every promise. His faithfulness does not depend on ours: if we are faithless, he remains faithful (2 Tim 2:13). God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son (1 Cor 1:9), and he will keep those he has called to the end (1 Cor 1:8). When God wanted to give his people the strongest possible assurance, he added an oath to his promise, so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement (Heb 6:18).

The attributes become our life. God does not reveal himself only so that we can admire him from a distance. He means us to trust him, worship him and become like him. We cannot share his eternity or his omnipresence. But by his Spirit we are being changed into the image of Christ (2 Cor 3:18), learning to be true, faithful, patient, merciful, just and loving in our small measure. Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children (Eph 5:1).

And one day we will see him. We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). The study of God's attributes is preparation for that day. All eternity will not exhaust them.
6.theology:
Faithfulness and assurance: The believer's security rests not on the strength of his grip on God but on God's grip on him. Because God is faithful, those he justifies he will also glorify (Rom 8:30). This is why true believers persevere: not because they are strong, but because he does not let go.

Communicable attributes and the Christian life: The attributes God shares with us are the outline of the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Gal 5:22-23). Growth in holiness is growth in likeness to God.

Knowing God and worship: Every attribute is a reason for praise. The Psalms rarely praise God in general. They praise him for something specific: his steadfast love, his faithfulness, his power, his justice, his works. Learning the attributes gives our worship words.
6.examples:
Then: Abraham was promised a son and waited twenty-five years. He and Sarah grew old, and the promise seemed impossible. Paul says that Abraham grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God, fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised (Rom 4:20-21). Faith is simply taking God at his word because of who he is.

Now: A widow keeps a notebook. Each morning she writes down one thing about God from her Bible reading and one way she has seen it that day. After a year she has a record of God's faithfulness in her grief, written in her own hand. Lamentations 3:23 is on the first page.

A simple test: Which of God's promises are you finding hardest to believe right now? What would it mean to trust the faithfulness of the One who made it?

verseByVerse.quote: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: These verses are the turning point of Lamentations. The poet has described his suffering in raw detail; he even says God has made my teeth grind on gravel (Lam 3:16). Then he calls something to mind and has hope. God's mercies are new every morning, like manna, enough for each day and no more. Faithfulness is not usually proved in a single dramatic rescue. It is proved in daily provision through long sorrow.

verseByVerse.quote: So when God desired to show more convincingly to the heirs of the promise the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath, so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God did not need to swear an oath. His word is enough. But he swore anyway, for our sake, to remove every possible doubt. Two unchangeable things, his promise and his oath, stand behind the hope of every believer. And note who receives this encouragement: those who have fled for refuge. Assurance is for those who have run to Christ, not those who trust in themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: if we are faithless, he remains faithful— for he cannot deny himself. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is part of a short hymn or saying. Its earlier lines carry warnings: if we deny him, he also will deny us (2 Tim 2:12). But the last line turns on God's character. Even when his people are weak and failing, he remains faithful, because he cannot deny himself. God's faithfulness is rooted in his own nature. He would have to stop being God to break his word.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children. And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul draws the practical conclusion of everything God is. Children resemble their father. Believers are called to imitate God, not in his incommunicable greatness, but in love: as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us. The attributes of God are most fully seen in the cross, and most fully imitated in self-giving love.

6.reflection:
Read Lamentations 3:1-33. How does the poet move from despair to hope?

Which of God's promises do you most need to rest on today?

Which of God's communicable attributes do you most want to grow in? What would one step look like?

Choose one attribute of God from this study and use it to shape your prayer of praise this week.
